concepts.name: Maximum Strength and Actual Composition of Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Constitutional ceiling: 550 elected + 2 Anglo-Indian nominated members (Article 81 & 331) vs. current effective strength post 104th Amendment abolishing Anglo-Indian nomination
Distinction between 'not more than 530' from states, 'not more than 20' from UTs, and the now-abolished nominated category
How delimitation and reorganisation of states affect seat allocation without breaching the constitutional ceiling
UPSC trap: 552 vs 550 vs 543 — which number applies in which context

concepts.name: 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 — Impact on Lok Sabha Composition
key_dimensions: Abolition of nominated Anglo-Indian seats in Lok Sabha (Article 331) and State Legislatures (Article 333)
Extension of reservation for SC/ST seats for another 10 years (until 2030) under Articles 334
Distinction: reservation of seats vs. special representation — what was abolished and what was extended
Comparison with 95th Amendment (extended OBC/SC/ST reservation in local bodies) to avoid confusion

concepts.name: Reservation of Seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Constitutional basis: Article 330 — reservation in proportion to population in each state/UT
Temporary provision originally intended for 10 years, periodically extended — current sunset via Article 334 post-104th Amendment (2030)
Seats are reserved within general constituencies, not separate electorates — distinction from Communal Award/Poona Pact concept
UPSC trap: No reservation for OBCs or minorities in Lok Sabha under the Constitution (only SCs and STs)

concepts.name: Territorial Constituencies and Delimitation for Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Article 82: Readjustment after each Census — Parliament by law delimits constituencies
Delimitation Commission: statutory body, orders have force of law, not subject to court challenge (Article 329)
Freeze on readjustment of seats: currently frozen till 2026 (based on 1971 Census) by 42nd and 84th Amendments — implications for southern states
Single-member territorial constituencies and the First-Past-the-Post system vs. proportional representation debate

concepts.name: Qualifications and Disqualifications for Lok Sabha Membership
key_dimensions: Article 84: Must be citizen of India, 25 years of age, and possess qualifications prescribed by Parliament (Representation of People Act)
Article 102: Disqualifications — holding office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, non-citizen, disqualified under any law made by Parliament
Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) as an additional ground of disqualification — decided by Speaker, not President
UPSC trap: President decides disqualification under Article 102 on Election Commission's advice EXCEPT for Tenth Schedule where Speaker decides

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule) — Application to Lok Sabha Members
key_dimensions: Grounds of disqualification: voluntarily giving up party membership OR voting/abstaining contrary to party whip without prior permission
Exceptions: merger of political parties (2/3rd members agree) — split provision was deleted by 91st Amendment, 2003
Role of Speaker as adjudicating authority — criticism of partisan role; Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan case upheld Tenth Schedule but made Speaker's decision subject to judicial review
Disqualification does NOT apply if a member is elected Speaker and resigns from party — special protection for Speaker's neutrality

concepts.name: Election of the Speaker of Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Article 93: Lok Sabha elects its own Speaker and Deputy Speaker from amongst its members — no external authority involved
Convention vs. Constitution: Constitution does not prescribe qualifications; convention dictates the ruling party nominates Speaker
Pro-tem Speaker: appointed by President, only to administer oath to new members and preside over election of Speaker — not mentioned in Constitution, a constitutional convention
UPSC trap: Speaker is elected by simple majority of members present and voting (not special majority); compare with removal which requires effective majority

concepts.name: Removal of the Speaker — Procedure and Conditions
key_dimensions: Article 94: Speaker can be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all then members of Lok Sabha (effective majority) — requires 14 days' advance notice
During pendency of removal resolution, Speaker cannot preside but can vote (UPSC trap: Speaker has no casting vote here, votes as a regular member)
Automatic vacation: Speaker vacates office immediately before the first sitting of new Lok Sabha (not at dissolution — continues till new House constitutes)
Comparison with removal of Deputy Speaker — identical procedure under Article 94

concepts.name: Powers and Functions of the Speaker of Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Presiding and conduct of business: final interpreter of Rules of Procedure, Constitution within the House — rulings not subject to appeal
Certification of Money Bills under Article 110 — Speaker's certificate is final and cannot be questioned in any court (Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha asymmetry)
Tenth Schedule adjudication: quasi-judicial role in disqualification proceedings — subject to judicial review only after final decision (Kihoto Hollohan)
Joint sitting of Parliament (Article 108): presided over by Speaker of Lok Sabha, not the President or Vice-President

concepts.name: Speaker's Casting Vote and Voting Rights
key_dimensions: Article 100(1): Speaker does NOT vote in the first instance but exercises a casting vote in case of equality of votes — unlike UK Speaker who never votes
Casting vote must be exercised judiciously — convention is to vote in favour of further discussion or status quo, not to make law
UPSC trap: During removal resolution against Speaker, Speaker can vote in the first instance (as a regular member), but has NO casting vote
Contrast with Rajya Sabha: Vice-President (Chairman) has no original vote, only a casting vote — same rule

concepts.name: Speaker's Role in Certifying Money Bills — Article 110
key_dimensions: Definition of Money Bill: Article 110 lists 7 specific matters (taxation, appropriation, Consolidated Fund, etc.) — a bill dealing with ONLY these is a Money Bill
Speaker's certificate: if Speaker certifies a bill as Money Bill, Rajya Sabha's role is limited to 14-day recommendation (not binding) — Lok Sabha supremacy
Controversy: Aadhaar Act, 2016 certified as Money Bill — challenged in Supreme Court; SC in Rojer Mathew case referred to larger bench — constitutionality of Speaker's certificate under scrutiny
UPSC trap: Finance Bill ≠ Money Bill; Finance Bill contains Money Bill provisions but also other provisions — Rajya Sabha has full powers over non-Money Bill parts

concepts.name: Duration of Lok Sabha — Normal Term, Extension, and Dissolution
key_dimensions: Article 83(2): Normal term is 5 years from date of first sitting after general election; President can dissolve earlier
Extension during National Emergency (Article 352): Parliament may extend Lok Sabha's term by one year at a time — no limit specified but must be discontinued within 6 months of Emergency ceasing

Dissolution vs. Prorogation vs. Adjournment: dissolution ends the House (all pending bills lapse except those passed by both Houses pending Presidential assent); prorogation ends a session; adjournment ends a sitting
UPSC trap: Rajya Sabha is never dissolved; Bills pending in Lok Sabha at dissolution lapse — but Joint Committee reports and Select Committee reports do NOT lapse

concepts.name: Quorum Requirements for Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Article 100(3): Quorum is 1/10th of total membership of the House — for Lok Sabha (543 members) this is approximately 55 members
In absence of quorum, Speaker must adjourn or suspend until quorum is present — no business can be transacted
UPSC trap: Quorum is 1/10th of TOTAL membership (not members present), and it's the same fraction for both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Difference from special majority requirements: Constitutional amendments (Article 368) require 2/3rd of members PRESENT AND VOTING plus majority of total membership

concepts.name: Vacation of Seats and Conditions for Disqualification from Membership
key_dimensions: Article 101: Double membership — a person cannot be member of both Houses simultaneously; if elected to both, must vacate one within 10 days
Absence without permission for 60 consecutive days leads to seat being declared vacant by the House (Article 101(4))

Resignation: member may resign by writing to Speaker; Speaker must be satisfied the resignation is voluntary and genuine before accepting (Supreme Court ruling in case of resignations during political crises)
UPSC trap: Disqualification under Article 102 ≠ disqualification under Tenth Schedule — different decision-making authorities (President vs. Speaker)

concepts.name: Privileges of Lok Sabha Members — Article 105
key_dimensions: Freedom of speech in Parliament: Article 105(1) — no member can be prosecuted in any court for anything said or vote cast in Parliament; Article 105(2) extends to committees
Limits: freedom of speech in Parliament is subject to rules of procedure and Article 121 (no discussion of conduct of judges of SC/HC in performance of duties)
Breach of privilege and contempt of House — House itself is the judge; no external court jurisdiction (PV Narasimha Rao case: bribery to vote exception)
UPSC trap: Parliamentary privilege protects what is said INSIDE Parliament; defamatory speech outside Parliament has NO protection and member can be sued

concepts.name: Pro-tem Speaker — Constitutional Status and Functions
key_dimensions: Not mentioned in the Constitution — a constitutional convention/practice followed since independence
Appointed by President to preside over first sitting of new Lok Sabha after general election; sworn in by President
Functions: administers oath/affirmation to newly elected members, presides over election of the new Speaker — ceases to hold office once Speaker is elected
UPSC trap: Pro-tem Speaker has all powers of Speaker during his tenure but conventionally exercises only the limited functions of oath administration and Speaker's election

concepts.name: Relationship Between Lok Sabha Speaker and Rajya Sabha Chairman
key_dimensions: Speaker is elected by Lok Sabha members; Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice-President) is elected by both Houses of Parliament sitting together — different electoral colleges
In joint sitting (Article 108): Speaker of Lok Sabha presides (NOT the Vice-President/Chairman of Rajya Sabha) — Lok Sabha Speaker has precedence
Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha presides if Speaker is absent from joint sitting; if Deputy Speaker is also absent, a person determined by joint sitting presides
UPSC trap: Vice-President/Rajya Sabha Chairman is NOT a member of either House; Speaker of Lok Sabha IS a member of Lok Sabha

concepts.name: Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha — Election, Powers, and Removal
key_dimensions: Article 93: Elected by Lok Sabha from amongst its members — same procedure as Speaker; by convention from opposition party (recent practice has deviated)
Powers: performs all functions of Speaker when Speaker's office is vacant or Speaker is absent; cannot be overruled by Speaker on any matter
Removal: identical procedure to Speaker — resolution with 14 days' notice, passed by effective majority (majority of all then members)
UPSC trap: Deputy Speaker presides over joint sitting if Speaker is absent, NOT the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman; also Deputy Speaker chairs Departmentally Related Standing Committees

concepts.name: Voting Mechanisms and Majority Types in Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Simple majority (ordinary majority): majority of members present and voting — used for ordinary bills, procedural decisions (e.g., electing Speaker)
Absolute majority: majority of total membership of the House (272+ in Lok Sabha of 543) — not explicitly used in Constitution but referenced in No-Confidence motion discussions
Effective majority: majority of all THEN members (excluding vacancies) — used for removal of Speaker, Deputy Speaker
Special majority under Article 368: 2/3rd of members present and voting + majority of total membership — for Constitutional amendments; some amendments additionally require state ratification

concepts.name: No-Confidence Motion Against the Council of Ministers — Lok Sabha Exclusivity
key_dimensions: Article 75(3): Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha ONLY — no-confidence motion can only be moved in Lok Sabha, not Rajya Sabha
Procedure: requires support of 50 members to admit the motion; if passed by simple majority, government must resign
Confidence motion vs. No-confidence motion: government can also seek confidence vote on its own; defeat on a confidence motion = defeat on no-confidence motion in effect
UPSC trap: Rajya Sabha has NO role in no-confidence motion; a government can survive even without majority in Rajya Sabha — this is the core asymmetry between the two Houses
